paragraphs: A reinforcement learning algorithm can perform very differently depending on its hyperparameters: settings chosen around the learning procedure. Small adjustments can produce large changes in results, and settings that work well in one environment may work poorly in another. This makes a strong reported score difficult to interpret without also understanding how much tuning it required.

The paper proposes an empirical methodology for studying that dependence across a chosen collection of environments. Its purpose is to make sensitivity something researchers can quantify and compare between algorithms. The approach therefore adds another dimension to evaluation: how performance responds to hyperparameter choices, alongside the performance achieved after tuning.

The authors demonstrate the methodology on several commonly used normalization variants of PPO. Their results suggest that some apparent algorithmic improvements may reflect greater reliance on tuning. This is a qualified empirical finding, rather than a claim that improvements generally disappear. It matters because an algorithm's best achievable result and its sensitivity to configuration describe different aspects of its usefulness.
neurips-2024-a-method-for-evaluating-hyp.tldr: The paper introduces a way to measure reinforcement learning algorithms' sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning and examines normalization variants of PPO.

paragraphs: When observations arrive sequentially, an uncertainty estimate needs to remain valid as more data accumulate. This paper develops a unified confidence sequence for self-concordant generalized linear models, covering examples such as Gaussian, Bernoulli, and Poisson models. The resulting confidence regions are convex, and the authors report numerical tightness that matches or improves on existing approaches.

The construction uses likelihood ratios and a time-uniform PAC-Bayesian bound, with uniform distributions serving as both prior and posterior. For Bernoulli models, the confidence radius avoids polynomial dependence on the norm of the unknown parameter. This removes a particular source of deterioration in the bound, without claiming that every form of parameter dependence disappears.

The authors apply these confidence regions to OFUGLB, an optimistic algorithm for generalized linear bandits. Its analysis achieves state-of-the-art regret guarantees across various self-concordant cases, including some with unbounded outcomes. For bounded cases, including logistic bandits, the guarantees also avoid polynomial dependence on parameter norm. Numerical logistic-bandit experiments show performance matching or exceeding prior algorithms.
neurips-2024-a-unified-confidence-sequen.tldr: A unified confidence-sequence construction yields tighter uncertainty estimates and strong regret guarantees for generalized linear bandits.

paragraphs: Online regression updates a prediction model as streaming observations arrive. The Passive-Aggressive method controls these updates using an error threshold: whether the prediction error crosses that threshold affects the response. Selecting the threshold is difficult, particularly when the model must account for side information and prediction tracking is only one part of the objective.

This paper introduces an adaptive framework that uses side information to make finer adjustments to the model's weight vector. It also selects the threshold adaptively, with a theoretical guarantee of convergence to the optimal setting. The contribution connects adjustment of the model itself with adjustment of the rule governing its updates.

The authors additionally provide an efficient implementation that substantially reduces computational complexity. Their numerical experiments report improved performance on criteria associated with the side information while keeping tracking error low. These results matter because they show that adapting to additional requirements can coexist with accurate tracking in the tested scenarios, extending the practical scope of the traditional Passive-Aggressive approach.
neurips-2024-adaptive-passive-aggressive.tldr: An adaptive Passive-Aggressive regression framework uses side information to refine updates and automatically select its error threshold.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks are often studied through the graph structures they can distinguish. This paper takes a different perspective: what happens to their real-valued classification outputs as the input graphs become larger? The setting considers graphs drawn from random graph models, allowing the authors to analyze prediction behavior as graph size grows.

For a broad class of networks, the authors prove that the output converges to a constant. The covered architectures include models using mean aggregation and the attention mechanism used by graph transformers. The results span several random graph families, including sparse and dense Erdős-Rényi variants, stochastic block models, and the Barabási-Albert model.

Convergence toward a constant restricts what these classifiers can express uniformly as graph size increases: their outputs eventually lose variation in the analyzed settings. Experiments support the theoretical findings and also observe this behavior on some real-world graphs. That empirical extension is narrower than a universal claim about real data; the paper identifies a broad asymptotic phenomenon, not failure of every graph classifier on every finite graph.
neurips-2024-almost-surely-asymptoticall.tldr: The paper proves that broad classes of graph neural classifiers approach constant outputs on growing graphs from several random graph models.

paragraphs: Retrieving 3D objects becomes challenging in an open-set setting where object-level labels are unavailable. The paper builds on a useful source of shared structure: objects from different categories can contain similar parts. Its HARF framework represents objects from the bottom up through assemblies of parts, aiming to make those commonalities useful for retrieval.

Two components address how assemblies can receive consistent representations. Hypergraph Isomorphism Convolution provides smoothing, while Isomorphic Assembly Embedding produces representations designed to align geometric and semantic information. A further component, Structure Fuzzy Reconstruction, uses higher-order relationships and fuzzy representations to address distribution skew. Its hypergraph construction combines correlations reflecting local certainty and global uncertainty.

The authors also construct three datasets with part-level annotations: OP-SHNP, OP-INTRA, and OP-COSEG. Experiments and ablation studies on these benchmarks show HARF outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines a representation strategy with evaluation resources: shared parts provide the basis for representing unfamiliar categories, while the hypergraph machinery captures relationships among their assemblies.
neurips-2024-assembly-fuzzy-representati.tldr: HARF uses shared object parts, hypergraphs, and fuzzy representations to improve open-set 3D object retrieval.

paragraphs: Adversarial attacks can alter an input in subtle ways that change a classifier's prediction. This paper approaches defense by separating factors responsible for the label from factors that help explain the input's appearance without determining its label. The intended behavior is to assign adversarial perturbations to the second group and base classification on the first.

CausalDiff adapts a diffusion model for conditional data generation and trains it toward a causal information bottleneck objective. That objective is designed to disentangle the two groups of factors. The approach therefore connects the generation of data with the information used for classification, aiming to preserve label-relevant information while separating nuisance variation.

Across the evaluated unseen attacks, the authors report stronger robustness than state-of-the-art defenses. Average robustness reaches 86.39% on CIFAR-10, 56.25% on CIFAR-100, and 82.62% on GTSRB, with reported improvements of 4.01, 3.13, and 4.93 percentage points respectively. These are empirical results supporting the proposed defense strategy; the factor-separation goal does not itself establish immunity to arbitrary attacks.
neurips-2024-causaldiff-causality-inspir.tldr: CausalDiff trains a diffusion model to separate label-relevant factors from nuisance factors, improving robustness across evaluated unseen attacks.

paragraphs: A language model produces a distribution over possible next tokens, and that distribution can be more or less concentrated. This paper investigates internal components that regulate this prediction uncertainty. It examines previously identified entropy neurons and introduces another group, called token frequency neurons, whose effects depend on how common individual tokens are.

Entropy neurons affect confidence indirectly. They write into an unembedding null space, meaning their contribution has little direct effect when internal representations are converted into token scores. Their activity nevertheless changes the residual stream's norm. Through the final LayerNorm, this can scale down the scores and alter the concentration of the output distribution. The authors observe these neurons in models up to seven billion parameters.

Token frequency neurons act differently: they raise or lower each token's score in proportion to its log frequency, moving predictions toward or away from the unigram distribution. A detailed induction case study, involving continuation of repeated subsequences, shows entropy neurons actively managing confidence. Together, these findings identify distinct mechanisms for reshaping next-token probabilities.
neurips-2024-confidence-regulation-neuro.tldr: The study identifies how entropy neurons and newly described token frequency neurons regulate language models' next-token probability distributions.

paragraphs: Adapting an agent to a new reward function requires understanding which behavior will produce valuable outcomes. Predicting the world one step at a time can accumulate errors over long horizons. Successor features offer another route by summarizing a policy's long-term state occupancy, making evaluation under new rewards simpler, although optimizing policies through those summaries remains challenging.

DiSPO learns a distribution of successor features associated with the behavior policy in a stationary dataset. It also learns a policy that can act to realize different successor features available within that dataset. This links a collection of long-term outcome summaries to behaviors that can pursue them, enabling a simple procedure for policy optimization across reward functions.

Because the model represents long-term outcomes directly, it avoids the compounding error associated with autoregressive rollouts. The authors implement the approach using diffusion models and provide theoretical and empirical support across simulated robotics problems. Its transfer capability is grounded in the outcomes represented in the dataset, which is central to how its zero-shot policy optimization operates.
neurips-2024-distributional-successor-fe.tldr: DiSPO models distributions of long-term outcomes and corresponding behaviors to enable zero-shot policy optimization across reward functions.

paragraphs: Regret measures how much a player could have gained by changing its decisions. Richer families of changes give stronger guarantees but can be harder to handle computationally. This paper develops algorithms between two existing extremes: full swap regret and the weaker linear-swap notion, using restricted families of deviations in extensive-form games.

The authors introduce k-mediator deviations and obtain regret-minimization algorithms requiring N^{O(k)}/ε² rounds. They also connect these deviations to low-degree polynomial changes of strategy. For degree k and game depth d, their bound is N^{O(kd)^3}/ε² under a constant branching factor. For fixed k, this gives polynomial bounds for Bayesian games and quasipolynomial bounds under the stated polylogarithmic-depth assumption.

A key simplification replaces a fixed strategy with a distribution whose expected change under a deviation is approximately zero. Finding this relaxed fixed point is efficient, whereas the corresponding actual fixed-point problem is shown to be PPAD-hard. A connection to low-depth decision trees helps characterize the deviations. The approach also yields a faster correlated-equilibrium algorithm in the stated medium-precision regime.
neurips-2024-efficient-phi-regret-minimi.tldr: Parameterized deviation families and fixed points in expectation enable efficient regret minimization between linear-swap and full swap guarantees.

paragraphs: Clinical questions can require combining information from discharge summaries spanning several hospital admissions. Benchmarks centered on single notes or narrow topics may not capture that work. EHRNoteQA is designed to evaluate language models on questions closer to these information needs, using discharge summaries from the MIMIC-IV electronic health record resource.

The benchmark contains 962 question-answer pairs. GPT-4 generates initial versions, which three clinicians then review and refine for clinical relevance. Questions cover eight topics and include cases requiring information across multiple summaries. Both open-ended and multiple-choice formats are provided, with an evaluation method for each. The authors test 27 models and examine factors such as summary length and number.

To assess practical relevance, the study compares benchmark performance with performance evaluated manually by clinicians. EHRNoteQA has stronger correlations than the other compared benchmarks, with Spearman correlation 0.78 and Kendall correlation 0.62. This supports its usefulness as a proxy for expert assessment in the examined setting. The result concerns the quality of evaluation, rather than establishing that the tested models are ready for autonomous clinical decisions.
neurips-2024-ehrnoteqa-an-llm-benchmark-.tldr: EHRNoteQA tests language models on clinically reviewed questions across discharge summaries and correlates well with clinician evaluations.

paragraphs: A graph's pattern of connections can carry bias into systems that learn from it. This matters for both existing networks and synthetic graphs generated for purposes such as privacy or scalability. The paper investigates how structural bias produces disparities in predictions about relationships between pairs of entities, and how graph generation can amplify that bias.

The authors first analyze the sources of these disparities theoretically. They then design a fairness regularizer to counter the identified factors. A regularizer adds a training preference that discourages particular unwanted behavior; here, the target is structural bias. The same design supports more than one use, including its integration into a generative model to form FairWire.

Experiments on real-world networks show effective bias mitigation for both real and synthetic graphs. The contribution joins diagnosis with intervention: the theoretical analysis identifies what to address, and the regularizer supplies a mechanism for addressing it during learning. The findings also make structural fairness relevant to graph generation itself, rather than only to predictions made after a graph has been created.
neurips-2024-fairwire-fair-graph-generat.tldr: FairWire uses a theoretically motivated fairness regularizer to reduce structural bias in real graphs and generated synthetic graphs.

paragraphs: Researchers can compare language models with brain activity by giving models the text that participants hear during an fMRI scan. Model representations then help predict the recorded brain signals. Earlier analyses often found similarly strong relationships in both hemispheres, creating a puzzle because language processing is classically associated more strongly with the left hemisphere.

This study examines whether model complexity changes that picture. It tests 28 pretrained models from eight families, ranging from 124 million to 14.2 billion parameters. In the analyzed dataset, the fit between model predictions and brain activity rises approximately linearly with the logarithm of parameter count. The study also relates this improvement to performance on natural language processing tasks.

Predictive fit improves in both hemispheres, but the improvement is stronger on the left. The left-right difference itself follows a scaling relationship with model size. These observations reconcile the model-based analysis with established evidence for left-hemisphere language dominance. The finding is about how well increasingly capable models predict brain responses, rather than evidence that those models reproduce the brain's underlying mechanisms.
neurips-2024-fmri-predictors-based-on-la.tldr: Larger language models predict language-related fMRI responses better, with stronger gains in the left hemisphere.

paragraphs: An ill-posed inverse problem can have several plausible reconstructions consistent with the same measurement. Returning a single image hides that ambiguity. A posterior distribution captures possible solutions and their probabilities, but its high dimensionality makes direct inspection difficult. This paper develops a way to summarize that uncertainty at several levels of detail.

The method predicts a tree that hierarchically summarizes the posterior for an input measurement. The hierarchy provides multiple granularities for examining possible reconstructions, rather than requiring all alternatives to be viewed at once. A neural network produces the entire tree in a single forward pass, making the summary itself the direct output of prediction.

Across diverse datasets and image restoration tasks, the authors evaluate both uncertainty quantification and visualization. Their method performs comparably to a baseline that generates samples with a diffusion-based posterior sampler and then clusters those samples hierarchically. It achieves this with orders-of-magnitude greater speed. The result suggests that useful hierarchical uncertainty summaries can be generated directly, substantially reducing the time needed for exploration in the tested settings.
neurips-2024-hierarchical-uncertainty-ex.tldr: A neural network predicts hierarchical trees of plausible reconstructions, providing posterior summaries much faster than a diffusion-sampling baseline.

paragraphs: The same action can affect different people differently. In reinforcement learning applications involving individuals, personal preferences or physiological differences can influence how states change over time. These differences matter for choosing effective personalized actions, but the factors responsible are often hidden rather than directly recorded in the available data.

The paper studies whether those latent factors and the individualized transition processes they influence can be identified from observed state-action trajectories. It establishes an identifiability result and introduces a practical learning method. Identifiability addresses a foundational question: whether the observations can distinguish the hidden structure the method aims to recover, rather than merely support a predictive fit.

Experiments across several datasets show that the method can identify latent transition processes and support learning individualized policies. The significance is the connection between understanding a person's response dynamics and adapting the policy used for that person. Personalization here concerns how actions change future states, so recovering individual differences in those dynamics directly informs the subsequent reinforcement learning problem.
neurips-2024-identifying-latent-state-tr.tldr: The paper establishes identifiability of hidden individual factors and learns personalized state-transition processes to support individualized reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Using a language model to generate crystals requires translating a three-dimensional structure into a one-dimensional sequence. That translation is complicated by the fact that one crystal can have multiple mathematical descriptions. If equivalent descriptions become different sequences, the representation preserves distinctions in notation that do not correspond to differences in the material.

Mat2Seq addresses this by converting equivalent descriptions of a crystal into a single unique sequence. The authors prove invariance to SE(3) transformations, covering rotations and translations, and to periodic descriptions. This gives the language model a representation that remains consistent under those changes. Prior approaches based on crystallographic information file streams do not ensure these properties.

Experiments combining Mat2Seq with language models show promising crystal-generation performance compared with earlier methods. The contribution has two distinct parts: a proven consistency property of the representation and empirical evidence for its usefulness in generation. Its central value is making the sequence correspond more directly to the crystal structure, reducing ambiguity introduced by the choice of mathematical description.
neurips-2024-invariant-tokenization-of-c.tldr: Mat2Seq gives equivalent crystal descriptions a unique invariant sequence and shows promising results for language-model-based crystal generation.

paragraphs: Generating personal mobility involves modeling people's activities and the patterns and motivations behind them. This paper uses a language model within an agent framework to handle that semantic information. The work focuses on aligning generated behavior with real activity data, making activity generation reliable, and exploring the resulting framework's uses in urban mobility analysis.

The framework incorporates individual activity patterns and motivations through two main mechanisms. A self-consistency approach aligns the language model with observed real-world activity data. A retrieval-augmented strategy supports interpretable activity generation by bringing retrieved information into the process. Together, these mechanisms connect the model's flexible handling of language with the empirical patterns it is meant to represent.

The authors evaluate the framework against state-of-the-art personal mobility generators and report evidence of its effectiveness. The stated contribution is an activity-generation framework grounded in real human activity data, with potential applications in urban analysis. Its importance lies in combining data alignment and interpretable generation within the same agent design, so that semantic modeling is tied to observed behavior.
neurips-2024-large-language-models-as-ur.tldr: An LLM agent framework combines data alignment and retrieval-augmented generation to model individuals' urban activities and mobility.

paragraphs: When many self-interested users share congested facilities, their choices can reduce overall welfare. Taxes can change those incentives, but choosing an effective tax is difficult when the designer has limited information. This paper studies equilibrium feedback: after deploying a tax plan, the designer observes only the Nash equilibrium that results.

The optimization problem combines an enormous space of possible tax functions with a nonconvex objective and unavailable gradients. The proposed algorithm approximates the optimal tax using piecewise-linear functions. It adds linear terms to ensure a strongly convex potential function and uses a dedicated subroutine to select exploratory taxes that reveal useful information about the game.

The authors prove that this computationally efficient procedure can find an ε-optimal tax with sample complexity O(βF²/ε), where β describes cost-function smoothness and F is the number of facilities. The result connects welfare optimization to the information obtainable from repeated equilibrium observations. It shows how structured tax choices and purposeful exploration can make learning feasible under the paper's restricted feedback model.
neurips-2024-learning-optimal-tax-design.tldr: A computationally efficient algorithm learns near-optimal congestion taxes using only the equilibria observed after tax deployment.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using data collected under another policy. Partial observability complicates this because observations do not directly reveal the underlying state. Treating an entire observation history as a state allows familiar methods to apply, but the resulting history-density ratios can grow exponentially with the horizon.

Future-dependent value functions offer an alternative. Earlier guarantees for memoryless policies use density ratios over latent states, avoiding the explicit history-ratio problem. This paper shows that other quantities in those guarantees, including the size of the future-dependent value function, can themselves grow exponentially with sequence length. The difficult dependence can therefore reappear elsewhere in the analysis.

The authors introduce coverage assumptions adapted to partially observable systems, including outcome coverage and belief coverage. Under these assumptions, they obtain polynomial bounds on the problematic quantities. Their analysis also produces new algorithms with complementary properties. The result clarifies both the promise and the requirements of the framework: avoiding exponential growth needs control of more than the latent-state density ratio alone.
neurips-2024-on-the-curses-of-future-and.tldr: The paper exposes hidden exponential terms in future-dependent off-policy evaluation and gives coverage assumptions that permit polynomial bounds.

paragraphs: Training an object detector with image-level labels provides useful weak supervision, but those labels do not precisely describe individual object boxes. This mismatch can hinder learning, especially when the detector needs to generalize across vocabularies. The paper introduces Language Hierarchical Self-training, or LHST, to use relationships within language to improve the supervision.

LHST expands the available image labels through a language hierarchy and couples that expansion with self-training. The expanded labels provide richer guidance and help reduce the mismatch between image labels and boxes. In the other direction, self-training estimates the reliability of expanded labels and selects among them. Each part therefore helps regulate the other.

The authors also use language hierarchy when generating prompts, aiming to bridge vocabulary differences between training and testing. Experiments across 14 object detection datasets show consistently superior generalization performance. The approach matters because it uses linguistic structure twice: to improve the labels guiding detector training and to connect the vocabulary encountered during training with the vocabulary needed at evaluation.
neurips-2024-open-vocabulary-object-dete.tldr: Language hierarchies improve weakly supervised detector training and prompt generation, strengthening generalization across 14 detection datasets.

paragraphs: Predicting where a pedestrian will move usually starts from a sequence of observed positions. Many datasets and methods assume that sequence is complete, even though occlusion, sensor failure, or a limited field of view can hide positions. This paper makes missing observations an explicit part of evaluating pedestrian trajectory prediction.

The authors introduce TrajImpute, a dataset that simulates missing coordinates with a uniform distribution of missing data within observed trajectories. They benchmark several imputation methods, which reconstruct absent coordinates, and then evaluate recent trajectory predictors using the reconstructed sequences. This connects the quality of filling gaps with the subsequent task of predicting future movement.

The work provides a shared resource for studying these two stages together and reports insights from the experimental comparison. Its controlled missing-data design is part of the evaluation setting: the simulated gaps follow the stated uniform distribution. The dataset is intended to support imputation-aware prediction research and could help move these methods toward applications where complete observation sequences cannot be assumed.
neurips-2024-pedestrian-trajectory-predi.tldr: TrajImpute benchmarks how reconstructing missing pedestrian positions affects subsequent trajectory prediction.

paragraphs: Robot learning data vary across bodies, sensors, and tasks, making it difficult to train a shared model. Collecting a separate dataset for each robot-task combination is expensive and can encourage overfitting. This paper investigates whether heterogeneous pretraining can instead learn policy representations that transfer across different robot embodiments and tasks.

Heterogeneous Pre-trained Transformers, or HPTs, align each embodiment's proprioceptive and visual inputs into a short token sequence. Proprioception describes information about the robot's own physical state. A large shared transformer trunk then processes these tokens, providing a common representation for policies controlling different robots. The architecture separates varied inputs from the shared processing that pretraining aims to improve.

The study explores scaling across as many as 52 datasets, drawing on real robots, simulation, deployed systems, and human video. HPTs outperform several baselines and improve fine-tuned policy performance by over 20% on unseen tasks across multiple simulation benchmarks and real-world settings. These findings support heterogeneous pretraining as a way to make diverse experience useful for later robot-policy learning.
neurips-2024-scaling-proprioceptive-visu.tldr: HPT shares a pretrained transformer across diverse robot inputs, improving fine-tuned performance on unseen tasks by over 20% in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Language models commonly group text into tokens because this improves performance, but tokenization also brings disadvantages. The paper highlights biases, adversarial vulnerability, weaker character-level modeling, and added complexity. SpaceByte explores whether a model operating directly on bytes can retain competitive performance while avoiding the separate subword tokenization step.

Its architecture starts with a byte-level transformer and inserts larger transformer blocks partway through the network. Those larger blocks run only after selected bytes, including spaces that often mark word boundaries. The central design choice is therefore where to spend additional computation within the byte sequence. The authors find that applying the larger blocks at these positions substantially improves performance.

Under fixed training and inference compute budgets, SpaceByte outperforms other byte-level architectures and approximately matches tokenized transformers. This comparison supports its ability to close the performance gap in the reported experiments. The result is especially relevant because the architecture preserves byte-level input while using boundary cues to decide when more substantial processing should occur.
neurips-2024-spacebyte-towards-deleting-.tldr: SpaceByte selectively applies larger transformer blocks at byte boundaries, roughly matching tokenized models under equal compute budgets.

paragraphs: A learner may train on one distribution and encounter a very different, potentially adversarial test distribution. This paper studies two ways to allow abstention in that setting. PQ learning permits abstaining on adversarial portions of test data, while TDS learning permits rejecting the entire test distribution when a shift is detected.

Earlier algorithms either relied on computationally difficult learning procedures or could reject everything after even a small shift. The authors address these issues for specified natural function classes, including intersections of halfspaces and decision trees, and standard training distributions such as Gaussians. They provide efficient PQ algorithms and TDS algorithms that tolerate moderate distribution shifts.

The technical core is an improved analysis of spectral outlier removal. It handles arbitrarily large outlier fractions and gives stronger control over polynomial moments after removal, supporting polynomial regression under shift. The techniques also yield results for tolerant testable learning and learning with nasty noise. These guarantees retain their framework-specific abstention options and the stated function-class and training-distribution setting.
neurips-2024-tolerant-algorithms-for-lea.tldr: Improved outlier-removal analysis yields efficient and more shift-tolerant learning algorithms in frameworks that permit abstention.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which observations to acquire so that each sample is useful. This paper studies a setting where the prediction targets are concrete, but sampling is restricted to an accessible region. Some targets can lie outside that region, so the learner must choose available observations according to how much they reveal about the targets.

The authors analyze a family of adaptive decision rules that aim to reduce target uncertainty. Under general regularity assumptions, they prove uniform convergence to the smallest uncertainty achievable from accessible data. The benchmark is therefore the best information available under the sampling restriction. It does not require every target's uncertainty to vanish when the accessible observations cannot fully resolve it.

The approach is demonstrated in active fine-tuning of large neural networks and safe Bayesian optimization. In those applications, the authors report strong sample efficiency and state-of-the-art performance. The contribution combines a theoretical account of what restricted sampling can accomplish with evidence that target-focused acquisition can use observations effectively in two practical learning settings.
neurips-2024-transductive-active-learnin.tldr: Adaptive sampling rules provably approach the lowest target uncertainty obtainable from accessible data under general regularity assumptions.

paragraphs: Generating a detailed 3D mesh from one image requires producing views and geometry that agree with each other. Earlier approaches can face long optimization times, inconsistent outputs, or insufficient resolution for intricate textures and shapes. Unique3D combines several stages to address fidelity, consistency, and efficiency within a single image-to-3D framework.

A multi-view diffusion model generates images from multiple viewpoints, while a corresponding normal diffusion model provides surface-orientation information. A multi-level upscaling process progressively increases the resolution of the orthographic views. The ISOMER reconstruction algorithm then integrates color and geometric priors into a consistent mesh, connecting the generated appearance information with the surface structure.

Experiments show that Unique3D substantially outperforms the compared image-to-3D baselines in geometric and textural detail. The framework's contribution is the coordination of view generation, resolution improvement, and mesh reconstruction. Each stage addresses a different part of the stated problem, allowing the final reconstruction to draw on both detailed visual information and explicit geometric guidance from the generated normal maps.
neurips-2024-unique3d-high-quality-and-e.tldr: Unique3D combines multi-view diffusion, normal maps, progressive upscaling, and mesh reconstruction to generate detailed 3D meshes from single images.
